newsitem.title: FALKLAND ISLANDS: Falklanders wary about UK Labour's victory.
newsitem.headline: Falklanders wary about UK Labour's victory.

text.p: Councillors in the disputed Falkland Islands on Friday reacted warily to the Labour Party's landslide victory in the British national election.
While they said they believed Labour's pledges that it would not hand the Falklands back to Argentina, they feared the new government would cultivate friendlier links with Buenos Aires.
One of the islands' most fervently anti-Argentine councillors Norma Edwards retracted her earlier decision to stand down and said she would fight a coming election to the eight-member legislature.
"With Labour in power, the Falklands need strong and experienced councillors," said Edwards.
"The Argentine government will be delighted with the Labour victory, seeing it being to their advantage in their long-standing sovereignty claim over the Falklands," she added.
Councillor Richards Stevens, a farmer, said he "feared the unknown" after nearly two decades of Conservative rule in Britain.
"Labour have not been in power for 18 years. We have to explain to them why we think direct links with Argentina are not desirable until Argentina drops its sovereignty claim," he said.

"My biggest worry is the loss of many good Conservative friends from parliament -- people who understood us and why we demand our right of self-determination," said another farmer and councillor, Eric Goss.

During the election campaign, Labour denied that it would hand the Falklands back to Argentina after Argentine Defence Minister Jorge Dominguez reportedly told Jane's Defence Weekly that he and Foreign Minister Guido Di Tella had met several Labour Party officials, including leader Tony Blair.
Labour also denied that Blair had meetings or discussions with Di Tella.
Britain and Argentina fought a 10-week war over the Falklands in 1982. Although Argentina lost, it maintains its claims to the sparsely populated archipelago which it calls Las Malvinas.

The two countries have restored diplomatic relations and in 1995 signed a deal to explore for oil in the waters around the Falklands, but fishing rights and sovereignty over the islands have been a stumbling block to closer ties.
